title: Farid: the crows and the eyes
hookLine: crows may peck the whole body, but spare the two eyes that hope to see the Beloved (Farid salok, ang 1382)
last: FARID — WHOM SHALL I CALL BAD.

lines: A LIGHT LEFT ON ALL NIGHT.
cards: A porch light left on all night. A chair turned toward the road. Someone has waited so long for a person to come home that the tea went cold and meals were forgotten.

Almost anything could go, except the view of the road, the one place the beloved would appear. Farid has a picture of that kind of waiting, and it's not gentle: a body, worn out, with crows landing on it.

teach.b: Near the end of his saloks, on Ang 1382, Farid paints himself as someone who has waited a whole life for God. In paraphrase: my body has dried to a skeleton, and crows peck at my palms; and still the Lord hasn't come.
Look at the fate of this servant. Then the next salok, in the original: kaagaa karang dhandholiaa sagalaa khaaiaa maas; e due nainaa mat chhuhau pir dekhan kee aas.
Crow, you've searched my skeleton and eaten all my flesh. But please don't touch these two eyes. I still hope to see my Beloved.

Crows and a skeleton are shocking at first. But it's the bride and her longing again, birha, from day two hundred forty-five, told in a stark picture. Everything can go: comfort, youth, strength, the body itself.

The one thing he asks to keep is the ability to look for the one he loves. Some readers hear more in the crows: all the things that pick at a life, worries, desires, the years, the world's small bites.
Let them take what they take.
Just keep the eyes, the part of you still turned toward God, or toward what's good, still hoping.

teach.h: AAS — HOPE TO SEE THE BELOVED.
teach.b: Pir here means the beloved, the husband, and for Farid, God. Aas means hope.
So the couplet ends not in despair but in hope, stubborn and alive, while there are still eyes to see.

how: Farid's saloks of longing, including the crow couplet, are sung in Sikh kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the Sufi who asked crows to spare his eyes
a Sikh Guru mourning a body lost in battle
a Hindu poet warning that death ends hope

games.q: inside Farid's couplet — tap the pairs.

s: it ends in hope: spare the eyes, I still hope to see my Beloved.
the couplet is another picture of birha, the longing of separation
the bride's waiting, told in a stark image.
Farid asks the crow to spare his hands
the crows peck his palms in the salok before; he asks them to spare his eyes.

games.q: you're Farid, worn to bone, and the crows have taken everything. what do you ask them to leave?
o: your two eyes, because you still hope to see your Beloved.
games.why: e due nainaa mat chhuhau pir dekhan kee aas: don't touch these two eyes; I still hope to see my Beloved.

practice: If you can, look out a window or up at the sky; if not, close your eyes and picture it. Let the day's worries be the crows, pecking at what they like for a minute.
Keep your gaze soft and open, with a little longing in it: for God, if you pray, or for goodness, peace, someone you love.

wordCard.voice: Farid. Here, his salok: crow, take my flesh, but spare these two eyes, for I still hope to see my Beloved.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: naina, eyes; e due nainaa, these two eyes, the one thing Farid asks to keep.

carryVoice: Your line: spare the eyes. Whatever the day takes, the eyes that hope can stay. Day two hundred sixty-one, done.
